items.title: Proton Drive’s Android App Uses Google ML Kit for Its Document Scanner
items.summary: Proton Drive’s Android app does ship Google’s ML Kit. It runs the document scanner Proton added in February, and nothing in the app’s code points it at the files you store. The alarm started on Mastodon. On Friday evening, 20 November, a user posting as Pretergeek shared a screenshot from App Manager, an Android tool that lists the components inside an app and flags known trackers. Two of the Google components it found in Proton Drive have names that start with “com.google.mlkit”, Google’s machine-learning kit for app developers. On Saturday the post took off. Reshares asking Proton for an explanation trended on infosec.exchange, and by 23:10 UTC the original had 361 boosts. Several replies said they were moving their files elsewhere. Proton’s Mastodon accounts hadn’t answered when we checked, and we found no coverage in major outlets. Proton Drive for Android is open source, so we read the code of the current public version, 3.3.1 from 2 November.

items.title: Cyberattack on Austrian Foreign Ministry Exposes Diplomatic Staff Data
items.summary: Austrian Foreign Ministry Hacked, Staff Contact Details Accessed Hackers accessed Austrian Foreign Ministry records containing staff contact details, including employees at diplomatic missions abroad. Austrian Foreign Ministry confirmed a cyberattack against its website that exposed staff contact information, including details of employees working at diplomatic missions abroad. The security breach occurred between November 12 and 13, during a global Microsoft outage , and raises questions about the security of government websites and the risks associated with services managed by external providers. According to the ministry, attackers gained unauthorized access to a website operated by an external service provider. The intrusion was detected on November 13, and authorities said they stopped it immediately. “”Between November 12 and 13, the foreign ministry’s website, which is operated by an external service provider, was accessed in an unauthorized ​manner,” the ministry said in a statement, adding that it happened ​during a global Microsoft outage .” Reuters reports . The ministry confirmed that the hack was detected on November 13 ⁠and government staff stopped it immediately. An investigation by a team of cybersecurity experts found that the intruders had viewed records containing the names and professional contact details of ministry employees. The information covered both staff at the ministry’s headquarters in Vienna and personnel working at Austrian diplomatic missions abroad. “An investigation by a team of experts ​found that during the unauthorized access, data records were viewed that listed ​the names and work contact details of employees at ministry headquarters as well as at diplomatic missions abroad,” the ministry added. The Austrian authorities have not disclosed how many records were accessed, whether the attackers copied the information, or how they managed to enter the website. They have also not identified the vulnerability or attack technique used. The ministry stressed that the incident did not affect citizens’ personal information. According to Austrian public broadcaster ORF , the authorities reported the incident to the Federal Office for Cyber Security and the Data Protection Authority, while also launching additional technical security checks. “The Foreign Ministry emphasized that it was taking the incident “very seriously.” The integrity of the infrastructure was of the highest priority. The systems were subject to strict security regulations and continuous monitoring, it stated. The incident had also prompted additional technical security checks.” states ORF . “The Foreign Ministry has been repeatedly targeted by cyberattacks. At the beginning of 2020, there was a serious cyberattack that lasted until February. In April 2022, there were cyberattacks involving phishing emails.” The timing of the incident is also noteworthy. The ministry said the intrusion coincided with a global Microsoft service outage, but it hasn’t established any connection between the two events. A major service disruption can complicate incident response and monitoring, but the available information doesn’t show that attackers exploited the outage to gain access. Attribution remains another unanswered question. The ministry hasn’t named any suspected country or threat group, and there’s no evidence linking this particular intrusion to a state-sponsored operation. However, the incident comes against a difficult diplomatic background. Austria has maintained military neutrality but has politically supported Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. In July 2026, Vienna publicly accused Moscow of being responsible for a cyberattack against the Foreign Ministry in late 2019 and early 2020, joining eight other EU member states in condemning Russian cyber operations. “The ministry did not suggest who might be responsible.” states Reuters. Russia has repeatedly rejected Western accusations of hacking. Diplomatic tensions have also increased following Vienna’s decision to expel four Russian diplomats in October, bringing the total number of Russian diplomats declared persona non grata by Austria since 2020 to 18. Moscow promised an appropriate response and subsequently expelled an Austrian trade delegate working at the country’s embassy in Russia. “Russia has repeatedly denied Western hacking allegations.” Reuters concludes . Beyond the political context, this incident offers an important security lesson. Government websites may not host classified information or directly manage critical services, but they can still expose information that attackers can use to target employees, build convincing phishing campaigns, identify diplomatic personnel or gather intelligence about government operations. The involvement of an external service provider also deserves attention. Outsourcing website management doesn’t outsource security responsibility. Public institutions need visibility into their suppliers’ security controls, access privileges, logging and incident response procedures, and must ensure that these arrangements receive regular independent checks. Names and professional email addresses might appear to be low-value information, but they can help attackers prepare highly targeted operations. In diplomatic environments, even basic contact details can provide useful intelligence for social engineering and further intrusions. Protecting government infrastructure also means protecting the people whose information and professional relationships can become the starting point for the next cyberattack. items.title: Cairn AI Framework Used in Autonomous Zero-Day Exploitation
items.summary: Amazon uncovered AI-powered attacks on universities, where autonomous agents found a zero-day and gained root access without human guidance. Amazon’s threat intelligence team found a Chinese-nexus actor running Cairn, an open-source AI pentesting framework, with one instruction for the agents: obtain shell access. No human chose the next step after that. The agents planned, executed, and adjusted on their own, and along the way they found a real zero-day in an open-source medical imaging application. The discovery happened because the operator left their own server exposed. On 10 September, Amazon spotted a publicly hosted Cairn instance running with no authentication, which meant anyone could see the project configurations, the prompts, and the AI’s output. The prompts were in Simplified Chinese, and script timestamps matched China Standard Time, over a roughly 48-hour campaign against university IP addresses in East Asia, outside mainland China. “On September 10, 2026, Amazon Threat Intelligence identified a server with a publicly hosted instance of Cairn, an open-source autonomous AI penetration-testing framework, running without authentication. Because the operator left the server publicly accessible, the operational history of the platform was visible to anyone on the internet, including project configurations, actor prompts, and AI output. The operator wrote prompts in Simplified Chinese, and the timestamps in executed scripts were configured to China Standard Time.” reads the report published by Amazon. “Analysis of the instance revealed a campaign targeting IP addresses associated with universities in East Asia outside mainland China over an approximately 48-hour period beginning September 8, 2026.” Not all targets were vulnerable. At one university, the agents found a Redis server that did not require a password. They spent about 16 hours trying 148 different actions to break in. These included using Redis replication to load code, bypassing its security protections, changing configuration files, damaging memory, and exploiting Log4Shell in a nearby service. When these attempts failed, they tried another approach. They exploited an SSRF vulnerability in a Qdrant server on the same network to explore internal systems. They then tried different passwords against PostgreSQL, SSH, and other services. None of these attempts succeeded, but the AI agents kept changing their tactics and trying new approaches. In another attack, the agents targeted a university GPU server for more than six hours. They collected about 80 real usernames from university websites, faculty directories, research lab pages, archived websites, and academic papers. They then tried more than 30,000 username and password combinations against SSH and other systems, including a VPN server and the university portal. These attempts also failed to gain access. The medical imaging target is where it worked. The agents mapped the application’s framework and API endpoints, found an upload parameter, tested it for path traversal, and had it: a working file-write vulnerability. From first mapping the API to writing arbitrary files took about 11 minutes. “Against a target running an open-source medical imaging AI application, the outcome was different. The agents identified the application’s framework, mapped its API endpoints, and found an upload endpoint with a filename parameter.” continues the report. “They tested that parameter for path traversal, and the parameter was vulnerable. In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server.” A later session turned that access into something worse. The agents wrote a Python reverse shell to sitecustomize.py, a file Python loads automatically on startup, then triggered a training endpoint that spawned a new process and imported the payload. That gave them a root shell with no human picking each step. Amazon assesses with high confidence this was a genuine zero-day, since no fix, advisory, or prior mention existed anywhere for the affected project. The human operator came back once the agents had proven the bug worked. They handed the agents a proxy tunnel into a second university’s network, where a server ran the same vulnerable software, and told them to use that foothold to reach other machines. Amazon infers the actor had already used the same zero-day to set up that tunnel, which means one AI-found bug became the key to a second network. Amazon notified the project’s maintainers, who shipped a fix and a security advisory. The affected universities weren’t AWS customers, so Amazon routed the warning through a government partner instead of reaching them directly. Separately, researchers at Gambit Security documented a different, financially motivated actor using the same framework against online retailers, so this isn’t a one-off experiment confined to espionage. The speed of these operations is the most important point. An AI agent that can find and exploit a zero-day in just a few minutes can move faster than most security teams can investigate a single alert. Even when the attacks failed, the agents kept working for 16 hours without breaks or time limits. Amazon uses honeypots and network traffic analysis to automatically detect some of this activity at no extra cost. The wider lesson is that defenders need to focus on reliable threat detection and fast responses. “To keep pace, organizations should prioritize high-confidence detections that trigger automated response, with humans overseeing outcomes rather than reviewing every individual action.” concludes the report. items.title: U.S. CISA adds Cisco Expressway, SAP NetWeaver, Broadcom VMware vCenter, and Apache Roller flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog
items.summary: U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) adds Cisco Expressway, SAP NetWeaver, Broadcom VMware vCenter, and Apache Roller flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added Cisco Expressway, SAP NetWeaver, Broadcom VMware vCenter, and Apache Roller vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog : CVE-2025-42884 SAP NetWeaver Improper Neutralization of Special Elements in Data Query Logic Vulnerability CVE-2026-76466 Cisco Expressway Series Use of Hard-coded Credentials Vulnerability CVE-2026-123890 VMWare vCenter Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel Vulnerability CVE-2026-129448 Apache Roller Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability The first vulnerability added to the catalog is CVE-2025-42884 (CVSS score of 6.5) , affecting SAP NetWeaver Enterprise Portal. The flaw allows an unauthenticated attacker to inject JNDI environment properties or provide a URL used during JNDI lookup operations. This could give the attacker access to an unintended JNDI provider and allow them to disclose or modify server information. CISA added the vulnerability to its KEV catalog on November 20, 2026, confirming that it has been exploited in the wild. However, no public reports have identified the attackers or provided details about the campaigns in which they used the flaw. The second vulnerability is CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS score of 9.8) , a critical flaw affecting Cisco Expressway Series. The vulnerability involves hard-coded credentials and insufficient validation of client certificates in clustered deployments. An attacker who obtains persistent cookies can connect to the device’s database service and execute specific remote procedure calls, potentially running arbitrary operating system commands with root privileges. According to cybersecurity firm F6, attackers exploited the flaw to breach clustered Cisco Expressway devices at a Russian organization shortly after a public proof-of-concept exploit became available. They then prepared tools for lateral movement across the victim’s network and accessed sensitive information. The activity has not been attributed to a known threat actor. The third vulnerability is CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS score of 9.8) , an authentication bypass affecting VMware vCenter. The flaw resides in the VMware Directory Service and allows an attacker with network access to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system. Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant linked its exploitation to ARMORY CASTLE , a suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group previously tracked as UNC5221. According to their investigation, the group exploited the vulnerability as a zero-day in early September 2026, before Broadcom disclosed and patched it. The attackers used a custom tool named BONESAW to obtain sensitive vCenter data, hijack the SAML Security Token Service and create an administrator account for persistent access. The campaign also involved the exploitation of a BeyondTrust Remote Support vulnerability, CVE-2026-102764. The fourth vulnerability is CVE-2026-129448 (CVSS score of 9.8) , a critical deserialization flaw affecting Apache Roller versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4. The issue affects the XML-RPC endpoint, which accepts and deserializes vendor extension types before authenticating requests. An unauthenticated remote attacker can exploit this behavior to execute arbitrary code on a vulnerable server. The Apache Roller maintainers have confirmed that attackers are exploiting the vulnerability in the wild, and CISA has added it to the KEV catalog. However, neither the project maintainers nor public reports have identified the threat actors behind these attacks or provided details about their targets and objectives. According to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 22-01: Reducing the Significant Risk of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities , FCEB agencies have to address the identified vulnerabilities by the due date to protect their networks against attacks exploiting the flaws in the catalog. Experts also recommend that private organizations review the Catalog and address the vulnerabilities in their infrastructure. CISA orders federal agencies to fix the vulnerabilities by November 23. items.title: GL.iNet Says Attackers Used Its Cloud Service to Plant Malware on Routers and KVMs
items.summary: GL.iNet, maker of the small travel routers many people use to run a VPN away from home, says an attacker used a hole in its cloud remote-management service to install malicious software on some of its routers and remote KVM devices. The company says it found the flaw on 20 November and closed it on discovery. Its security notice doesn’t say how many devices were hit, when the attacks began or what the malware does. On Saturday, 21 November, owners began receiving the notice by email, and GL.iNet released fixed firmware for its Comet KVMs. Router owners have a check, a reset instruction and a promise of new firmware. The KVMs are the more alarming half. A Comet sits between you and a computer, so whoever controls it sees that computer’s screen and types on its keyboard. When we published, the incident had been discussed on GL.iNet’s own forum, Hacker News and the Privacy Guides forum. We found no news coverage.

items.title: Internet Shutdowns in 2026: Every Government Cut-Off So Far (Tracker)
items.summary: In 20 countries, governments cut the internet or blocked major apps at some point in 2026 so far. Iran alone spent more than 100 days almost completely offline. This page lists every government-ordered shutdown and platform block we could document between 1 January and 20 November 2026: where and when it happened, what was cut, the reason given or reported, and whether a VPN could have helped. Each entry rests on public evidence from network monitors such as Cloudflare Radar and IODA, digital rights groups such as Access Now and SFLC.in, official notices and news reports. The yearly count of the #KeepItOn coalition arrives around March. Until then, this is the running tally for 2026, and we update it every month. Key findings 20 countries cut the internet or blocked major platforms in 2026 so far: 66 separate episodes started between 1 January and 20 November, and 8 older ones were still in force. Iran was offline for more than 100 days : about three weeks during the January protests and 88 days from the start of the war on 28 February. Access since then is slowed and tiered. Exam cheating is still a reason to switch off a country : Iraq did it at least 34 times, Sudan 10 times. Syria held its exams without a shutdown for the first time in at least a decade. Telegram was blocked by four governments (Russia, India, Iraq and Jordan), Iraq twice. A VPN would not have helped in 18 of the 66 episodes : the whole internet was off. In another 7, VPNs themselves were the target. 2026 edition, data to 20 November 2026. Next update: December 2026.

items.title: PHP2Shell aftershock: 18 more PHP flaws put enterprise web admins on alert
items.summary: PHP continues to root out flaws in its architecture, this week releasing fixes for a slew of additional security issues in the wake of PHP2Shell. The patches address 18 vulnerabilities , including a critical request smuggling flaw that could allow unauthenticated attackers to remotely execute code on vulnerable servers. Other vulnerabilities affect PHP’s core engine, session handling, process manager, and Common Gateway Interface (CGI) protocol, which bridges web servers with external application programs. The updates were released for all supported PHP versions, with PHP 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, and 8.2.36 containing the fixes. The disclosure comes as enterprises continue to grapple with the full impact of PHP2Shell , a pair of 9.2-severity-rated vulnerabilities disclosed in October. The flaws prompted the outright shutdown of some government websites, and, by some estimates, have borne the brunt of millions of exploit attempts . “Enterprises should read this release as PHP2Shell’s aftershock: Smaller, but it shakes the same walls,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research. Flaws enabling RCE, DoS, memory corruption One of the most serious flaws disclosed this week, CVE-2026-129289 , is rated a critical 9.2 on the Common Vulnerabilities Scoring System (CVSS). The request smuggling vulnerability impacts PHP-FPM, a background service that executes code for high-volume websites and apps. If exploited, the flaw could allow unauthenticated actors to execute PHP code remotely on vulnerable servers that reuse connections to PHP-FPM under certain conditions. It impacts specific nginx, Apache, HAProxy, and LSAPI configurations that reuse backend connections to PHP-FPM. When paired with a code execution bug, it can “ carry an attacker from the web worker toward the whole server,” Dickson explained. Several of the other patches also address vulnerabilities that could allow remote code execution (RCE). Still others address issues including information disclosure, memory corruption, denial-of-service (DoS) interruptions, potentially unsafe handling of HTTPS and FTPS URLs, and cross-site scripting. While there may be heavy focus on the 9.2-rated CVE-2026-129289, the lesser flaws still matter, Dickson said. For instance, in one case, one capital letter turned off encryption; a URL written as HTTPS:// or FTPS:// with an uppercase S could send passwords, tokens, form data, and files in plaintext, even through a redirect, to anyone watching the network. Not quite PHP2Shell level, but still high priority An attacker who exploits a PHP code-execution flaw gains access to whatever the PHP worker can touch, “which is just about everything,” Dickson said. Successful exploitation executes code with the privileges of the PHP worker, which holds the database password, API keys, cloud credentials, and session data. For example, he described what he called an “ugly” attack path: The threat actor gets in through the web application. Reads the configuration file; Dumps the customer database; Plants a web shell to come back later. He pointed out that PHP warned that PHP2Shell puts every installation serving web requests at risk, with no login required. “This release returns to the same neighborhood: session upload progress, fatal error backtraces, and how PHP behaves when it runs out of memory,” he said. Fritz Jean-Louis , principal cybersecurity advisor at Infotech, agreed that this is a high-priority patching event, if not a PHP2Shell-level emergency. Although several of the critical vulnerabilities require specific configurations or uncommon deployment scenarios, “they still affect one of the most widely deployed web runtimes in the world,” he noted. RCE is the most concerning outcome, as it can give an attacker control over the application server. From there, they may be able to access sensitive business data, steal credentials or session tokens, deploy persistent backdoors, modify application behavior, or use the compromised system as a foothold for deeper intrusion. “Even vulnerabilities that appear less severe, such as information disclosure or memory corruption, can become highly impactful when chained together by a determined attacker,” Jean-Louis said. What enterprises should do now Dickson emphasized the a PHP version number alone will not tell security teams whether they are exposed. Checking the version number is the easy part, but Linux distributions often backport fixes without changing the version string, so the package changelog tells more than the version number does. The hard part is finding every copy: Web servers, containers, hosting control panels, and appliances can all quietly bundle PHP, Dickson said. Then check the settings that matter: Is session upload progress on? Do PHP 8.5 workers include arguments in error backtraces? Does php-cgi face the internet? Is the PHP-FPM status page reachable from outside? He advised security teams to start with internet-facing PHP 8.5 servers, anything with session upload progress enabled, and any setup where several applications share one session store. PHP 8.5 should be first because it is the only branch exposed to the new backtrace flaw, and fatal error backtraces are on by default there, he explained. “Then patch everything else on a normal fast cycle,” Dickson said. He pointed out that PHP 8.2 has just six weeks to live; it will receive no security fixes after December 31, 2026. That means this release may be one of the last it receives. Running 8.2 into January is a risk decision; PHP 8.1 and older, meanwhile, receive no fixes from the PHP project. Interestingly, PHP’s advisory for the new PHP 8.5 backtrace flaw says a change in 8.5.12, the PHP2Shell release, is what made the new attack path reachable. “Emergency fixes are built fast, and fast work sometimes creates a new vulnerability ,” Dickson noted. In light of this, his advice is to preserve the PHP inventory built for PHP2Shell, “and keep it current,” because no one ever said during an incident, “We knew about too many of our PHP servers.” Understanding everywhere PHP runs Jean-Louis agreed that security teams should immediately inventory all PHP deployments, including those embedded in vendor products and appliances. They should also prioritize internet-facing systems, verify PHP-FPM and session management configurations, and deploy the latest supported PHP versions “as quickly as operationally feasible.” Organizations should view this as a continuation of the lesson learned from PHP2Shell, he said: Runtime vulnerabilities deserve the same attention as application vulnerabilities. While PHP2Shell was more “immediately exploitable” and quickly attracted real-world attacks, this release reinforces the need for strong asset inventory, rapid patch deployment, and visibility into underlying software components. “The biggest question for CISOs is not whether they run PHP; it’s whether they know everywhere it runs,” Jean-Louis said.

items.title: CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud
items.summary: The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com , a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed. A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com. The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands. “Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.” But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media , but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company]. The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors. The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260. The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260. Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria . Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data. Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.” A portion of the proposal that RansomwareHelp sent to a victim accounting firm in March 2024. Click to enlarge. The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.” “Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed. Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network. A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked. items.title: F5 scrambles to fix more critical BIG-IP security flaws
items.summary: F5 has released a batch of out of band patches for BIG-IP Access Policy Manager (APM) and BIG-IP iRule programmable scripting, five of which are rated 9.8 (Critical) in severity. BIG-IP Access Policy Manager (APM) is the vendor’s application access management and security product while BIG-IP iRules lets network administrators customize how BIG-IP handles application traffic. All five of the patches are stack-based buffer overflows that could let an unauthenticated threat actor terminate the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) and execute code remotely on vulnerable systems. F5 described them as follows: CVE-2026-121805 : When an iRule that processes client traffic using the PEM:subscriber command is configured on a virtual server, undisclosed requests can cause the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) to terminate and may lead to remote code execution (RCE); CVE-2026-120292 : When an HTTP profile and an iRule using the MR:message route command are configured on a virtual server, undisclosed requests can cause the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) to terminate and may lead to remote code execution (RCE); CVE-2026-120285 : When an HTTP profile and an iRule containing the PSC:ip_address command are configured on a virtual server, undisclosed requests can cause the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) to terminate and may lead to remote code execution (RCE); CVE-2026-116953 : When an iRule that processes client traffic using the GENERICMESSAGE:route command is configured on a virtual server, undisclosed requests can cause the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) to terminate and may lead to remote code execution (RCE); CVE-2026-123637 : When BIG-IP APM is provisioned and a per-request policy that includes the Client Information agent and Endpoint Security agents is applied to a virtual server, undisclosed requests can cause the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) to terminate and may lead to remote code execution (RCE). The company said there are no mitigations for the flaws and advised customers to install the hotfixes on vulnerable devices, and to upgrade vulnerable versions without a listed fix to a patched version. In the same batch of out of band patches, F5 also addressed CVE-2026-126822 , a high severity integer underflow vulnerability in BIG-IP APM SAML that could also crash TMM and lead to denial of service. This is the second critical issue in two months for APM; September’s zero-day bug was already being exploited when it was patched. F5 did not indicate that any of the current batch is as yet being exploited but given the growing trend of attacks on edge devices by criminals and nation-state threat actors, admins should update systems as soon as possible.
